Climate Change Conundrum: Economy v. Environment

By: John Webb | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
South Africa is hoping for a "Just Transition" to a greener future but, in a world turning its back on fossil fuels, will it risk pariah status as a result?

Unique Selling Point:
SA's Climate Change Conundrum: What Price Choosing Economy over Environment? A landmark court case in the Netherlands has shone a light on the limitations of companies and governments to determine when and how they move away from fossil fuels. We talk to leading experts in their field to show how South Africa's own ambition for a Just Transition to a greener future, in which job creation and economic growth compete with environmental imperatives, might be stymied by global climate change dictat.

Summary:
Last week marked an historic moment in the battle against climate change: for the first time in history a court ruled that a private company must cut its greenhouse gas output. Royal Dutch Shell was told by the Hague District Court to reduce its emissions by a massive 45% by 2030. It’s a ruling that could have implications globally, marking a new era in which not only governments but private companies are forced to cut their emissions. It follows to significant natural gas discoveries off the SA coasts by French firm, Total. It's argued oil and gas production would dramatically reduce South Africa’s current reliance on imports, create employment opportunities and provide an alternative to the current coal dominated energy sector. The Integrated Resource Plan, our energy blueprint, provides for 3000 MW of natural gas by 2030, seeing the commodity as the idea partner for its renewable energy ambitions. The IRP also makes allowance for 1500MW of new "clean" coal-fired power - an indication, say critics, of the lip service being paid to the Just Transition. This insert looks at the global move away from fossil fuels and how – as last week’s court ruling shows – it is no longer being left to the goodwill of even private entities. It also examines the impact of decisions often taken in the developed north on countries yet to fully reap the benefits of their own natural resources. Can a country like South Africa, grappling with some of the highest levels of unemployment in the world and stagnant economy, be expected to commit to “net zero”? And is it right that private companies be compelled to walk away from investments that might help a country like South Africa dig itself out of a large financial hole? Or is there a bigger picture that can’t be ignored? A planet heating at a rate that requires enormous commitment and sacrifice to reverse?

SCRIPT - Climate Crisis and Just Transition.
VO: South Africa is the world’s 12th largest greenhouse gas emitter, our per capita or per person emissions are higher than countries like China and India. So, we’ve joined the global move towards “Net Zero” – the point where humans stop adding to climate-heating gases in the atmosphere – by 2050.

ITV UPSOUND [00:01:31:09 - 00:01:32:17] Are we good? Yes. Look at the camera…

VO: We produce between 80 and 90% of our electricity from coal, and energy and heat production account for almost 40% of our total greenhouse emissions. If we’re serious about decarbonisation, it’s the obvious place to start.

ITV Aldworth Mbalati [00:22:23:03 - 00:22:49:24] We have to be responsible in terms of making sure that we do good to the environment.

VO: Aldworth Mbalati is an industrialist with dreams of helping revolutionise the country’s energy sector.

ITV Aldworth Mbalati [00:22:23:03 - 00:22:49:24 It is highly possible that you can do good business in an environmentally friendly way.

VO: And, says Mbalati, that’s what’s on offer from a commodity often referred to as the “cleanest fossil fuel”: Natural Gas. Compared to coal, it emits about 45% less Carbon Dioxide - the primary greenhouse gas generated by human activity. Natural Gas, according to the brochures, is the ideal partner for renewable sources of energy like wind and solar.

ITV Aldworth Mbalati [00:10:54:03 - 00:11:25:08] STRAP “Group Chief Executive, DNG Energy” You have sun during the day.You've got wind that predominantly flows at night. So, what do you do to balance that? (CUT) In order for renewables to truly shine, they need an anchor that pieces everything together in order to achieve what you call consistent baseload.

VO: Government’s Integrated Resource Plan or IRP sees gas providing 3000 MW of new electricity capacity – crudely, enough to power 2 million homes. The IRP is our electricity generation plan up to 2030, and while some analysts believe it’s unlikely we’ll reach that gas target, they’re not completely writing it off. They argue Natural Gas could be used for so-called flexible generation – coming on stream when wind and solar aren’t available.

Claire Question: Does that not fly in the face of our fossil fuel commitments?

ITV Dr Roland Ngam [00:11:00:12 - 00:11:35:10] The reason why the South African government wants to exploit these resources is because there is a glut of gas that is being discovered on the East Coast and even in the Karoo and in the Okavango. They have projects popping up everywhere (CUT) it is the kind of mentality, frankly, that you will see everywhere in the world.

VO: It’s not a mentality that impresses Dr. Roland Ngam, of political education institute, the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation. The main component of Natural Gas is methane, a greenhouse gas more potent than CO2. A cleaner fossil fuel in some respects but a fossil fuel it remains.

ITV Dr Roland Ngam [00:12:41:23 - 00:13:19:17] STRAP “Programme Manager: Climate Justice & Socioecological Transformation, Rosa Luxemburg Foundation” Well, they say that it is cleaner, but at the same time, you need to look at the entire footprint.

VO: A lobbyist for climate justice, Dr. Ngam is, in many ways, Mbalati’s opposite. They represent competing interests in a fast-changing world of other competing interests. A world where economics and the needs of the environment collide.

Upsound UN [09:37 – 09:45]: “You have been telling us… didn’t hear”.

VO: In early August, the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change released its most up to date study on the impact of global warming. It made disturbing reading: the planet is experiencing nearly unprecedented rising temperatures and carbon concentration levels and humans are, without doubt, the cause. (PAUSE) Action is needed to drastically cut emissions but, in a country like South Africa, that is far easier said than done.

ITV Barbara Creecy [00:17:39:09 - 00:18:22:19] I guess if I wanted an easy life, I would have chosen a different career.

LINK: Barbara Creecy has a tough job on her hands: as Environment Minister, her ambition to help avoid a climate catastrophe needs to take into account the many other challenges this country is facing. (Edit Note 6)

VO: More than 7 million South Africans were without jobs in the first 3 months of this year, a staggering unemployment rate of close to 33%. As it tries to cut emissions, government needs to figure out how not to add tens of thousands of coal chain workers to those stats.

ITV Barbara Creecy [00:08:08:12 - 00:08:43:18] what we have to ensure as we transition is that we can't leave people behind. And we can't say that sections of our society must bear the burden of this transition as opposed to other sections of society.

VO: Transition is the word used to describe the migration from fossil fuels to low or Zero Carbon. Or, more accurately, “Just Transition”

ITV Dr. Roland Ngam [00:00:25:15 - 00:00:37:21] What does this mean? This means that all the people who are going to be laid off, for example, if a coal mine closes down, all the people who live in the town that depends on all the business that comes from the coal mine. (CUT) All these constituencies need to be taken care of.

VO: Get it wrong in places like the Mpumalanga coal belt, home to the communities most likely to bear the human cost of the energy shift, and risk dire consequences.

LINK: Critical to any Just Transition is the concept of a social compact – agreement reached through dialogue and compromise - that pays special attention to the communities most impacted by the move away from fossil fuels. Very often, these are people on the margins and, as the events that unfolded on our streets in July demonstrated, ignoring their needs can have devastating consequences.

VO: Like so much else in the climate change space, it’s a contested idea.

ITV Aldworth Mbalati [00:25:45:21 - 00:26:16:04] Look, I understand what the concept is trying to achieve (CUT) In my mind, what you should be saying is what are the resources that we have available to us today that we can use effectively today in order to not destroy our environment but achieve our growth objectives. (CUT) [00:15:51:23 - 00:16:23:12] We need to achieve high economic growth rates. We need to achieve what we call a better world for all our citizens.

ITV Dr Roland Ngam [00:02:40:05 - 00:03:14:13] in principle, South Africa is committed to a just transition, but it is more complicated than that in reality.

VO: And not just because of our fragile economy or our reliance on coal to produce electricity…

ITV Melissa Fourie [00:03:28:22 - 00:03:35:03] I'm Melissa Fourie, and I'm the Executive Director of the Center for Environmental Rights.

VO: …but because those deciding policy aren’t always pulling in the same direction.

ITV Melissa Fourie [00:19:03:12 - 00:19:38:20] like with all transitions, there is a fundamental tension between those with vested interest in the status quo, in this case, the coal in particular (CUT) and those who can see the significant benefits of leaving behind that status quo and moving South Africa to a Zero Carbon future.

VO: That’s evident in the IRP. It says: “coal will continue to play a significant role in electricity generation in South Africa in the foreseeable future”.

Upsound Gwede Mantashe [00:00 – 00:12] “If we agree… of our lives.”

VO: While the IRP does aim to substantially reduce our reliance on coal and increase the share of renewables in our energy mix, it also plans 1,500 MW of new, “clean” coal-fired power- enough for about a million homes. And, while funders increasingly turn their backs on coal – clean or otherwise – Minister Gwede Mantashe appears resolute.

Upsound Gwede Mantashe [02:57 – 03:04] “We can… fresh air” [03:10 – 03:15] “What is… starving”

VO: Spare a thought for Minister Creecy, whose job it is to convince international financiers of our commitment to cut emissions. And get them to part with their cash.

ITV Barbara Creecy [00:09:54:07 - 00:10:29:14] STRAP “Minister of Environment, Forestry and Fisheries” we're no longer in a situation where climate change is a theory. We are living through the reality of it. We've had terrible droughts in our country. We've had raging fires. We've had extreme storms. All of this costs money and what we what we understand in the international arena is that unless there is a predictable and transparent source of financing (CUT) the consequences for developing countries are extremely serious.

VO: And so, she’s taking up the cause of developing countries and asking rich nations to make good on their pledge for so-called green funding, and to commit to a new goal of mobilising $750 billion dollars a year by 2030. In return, developing countries must show a commitment to decarbonisation and here, South Africa might just have an unexpected ace up its sleeve.

ITV Melissa Fourie [00:05:38:18 - 00:06:27:22] ironically, South Africa's heavy dependence on coal is actually positive at this very moment from a global point of view. Being able to remove greenhouse gas emissions from South Africa's coal power stations would result in reductions of carbon dioxide that is globally significant.

VO: Eskom is the country’s biggest greenhouse gas emitter, pumping around 213 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent into the atmosphere every year - exactly what a world banking on carbon neutrality should be looking for. If it follows through on plans to shut down most of its coal-fired power stations and move into the renewable space could Eskom be the spark that ignites a true Just Transition to a low carbon future?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): South Africa is hoping for a "Just Transition" to a greener future but, in a world turning its back on fossil fuels, will it risk pariah status as a result?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: SA's Climate Change Conundrum: What Price Choosing Economy over Environment? A landmark court case in the Netherlands has shone a light on the limitations of companies and governments to determine when and how they move away from fossil fuels. We talk to leading experts in their field to show how South Africa's own ambition for a Just Transition to a greener future, in which job creation and economic growth compete with environmental imperatives, might be stymied by global climate change dictat.
metadata.Summary: Last week marked an historic moment in the battle against climate change: for the first time in history a court ruled that a private company must cut its greenhouse gas output. Royal Dutch Shell was told by the Hague District Court to reduce its emissions by a massive 45% by 2030. It’s a ruling that could have implications globally, marking a new era in which not only governments but private companies are forced to cut their emissions. It follows to significant natural gas discoveries off the SA coasts by French firm, Total. It's argued oil and gas production would dramatically reduce South Africa’s current reliance on imports, create employment opportunities and provide an alternative to the current coal dominated energy sector. The Integrated Resource Plan, our energy blueprint, provides for 3000 MW of natural gas by 2030, seeing the commodity as the idea partner for its renewable energy ambitions. The IRP also makes allowance for 1500MW of new "clean" coal-fired power - an indication, say critics, of the lip service being paid to the Just Transition. This insert looks at the global move away from fossil fuels and how – as last week’s court ruling shows – it is no longer being left to the goodwill of even private entities. It also examines the impact of decisions often taken in the developed north on countries yet to fully reap the benefits of their own natural resources. Can a country like South Africa, grappling with some of the highest levels of unemployment in the world and stagnant economy, be expected to commit to “net zero”? And is it right that private companies be compelled to walk away from investments that might help a country like South Africa dig itself out of a large financial hole? Or is there a bigger picture that can’t be ignored? A planet heating at a rate that requires enormous commitment and sacrifice to reverse?
